headline: Less river water, fewer planted acres: Pinal County farmers adjust
dek: With Arizona's share of the Colorado River cut back, growers south of Phoenix are leaving fields empty, pumping more groundwater and rethinking what they plant.
body: For decades, canals carrying Colorado River water made the desert between Phoenix and Tucson one of the state's busiest farming areas. In recent years that supply has shrunk. A long drought and falling levels at Lake Mead led to shortage declarations on the river, and Arizona, which has the most junior rights among the lower-basin states, absorbed the deepest cuts.

Farms in Pinal County, which relied on the Central Arizona Project canal, have felt it most. Many growers have stopped receiving project water for irrigation altogether. Some have left part of their land fallow. Along the county's back roads, fields that once grew cotton, alfalfa or grain now sit bare.

Others have turned to groundwater. State and federal programs have helped pay for new wells and pipelines, but running the pumps takes energy and money, and the aquifers are not unlimited. Farmers and water managers alike describe groundwater as a bridge, not a lasting replacement.

The cuts are also changing what gets planted. Some growers are moving away from thirsty crops and toward ones that need less water or can be grown in fewer months of the year, and several are trying drip irrigation and other water-saving methods on fields that were flood-irrigated for generations.

Arizona, the other river states and the federal government continue to negotiate how the river will be shared in the years ahead. Until those talks finish, growers say, planning even one season ahead has become harder, and the effects reach well beyond the farm gate, to the dairies, feed suppliers and food businesses that buy from them.
